items.readable_text:
Content:
If a rational expression is expressed in factored form, we can sometimes make the expression even simpler by pulling out factors that are common in both the numerator and denominator.

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to simplify the rational expression

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{4(2x-3)}{2}.]

Content:
If we decompose [MATH: 4] into [MATH: 2\cdot 2,] we can pull out a factor of [MATH: 2] from both the numerator and denominator:

Content:
[MATH: (4(2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2)/(2) ⋅ (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1).]

Content:
The fraction [MATH: \dfrac{2}{2}] is the same as [MATH: 1,] and anything times [MATH: 1] is just itself, so

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(2) ⋅ (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1)|=; 1 ⋅ (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1)|=; (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1); 2(2x − 3).]

Content:
Note: There is a shortcut! We can just "cancel" a [MATH: 2] from the numerator and denominator.

Content:
[MATH: (4(2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1)|=; 2(2x − 3).]

Then, we cancel out all the pairs of common factors in the numerator and denominator. In this case, there are two pairs of [MATH: 2]'s.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If a rational expression is expressed in factored form, we can sometimes make the expression even simpler by pulling out factors that are common in both the numerator and denominator.

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to simplify the rational expression

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{4(2x-3)}{2}.]

Content:
If we decompose [MATH: 4] into [MATH: 2\cdot 2,] we can pull out a factor of [MATH: 2] from both the numerator and denominator:

Content:
[MATH: (4(2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2)/(2) ⋅ (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1).]

Content:
The fraction [MATH: \dfrac{2}{2}] is the same as [MATH: 1,] and anything times [MATH: 1] is just itself, so

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(2) ⋅ (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1)|=; 1 ⋅ (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1)|=; (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1); 2(2x − 3).]

Content:
Note: There is a shortcut! We can just "cancel" a [MATH: 2] from the numerator and denominator.

Content:
[MATH: (4(2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(2)|=; (2 ⋅ (2x − 3))/(1)|=; 2(2x − 3).]

---

Item 2 — Example: Simplifying Rational Expressions with Common Constant Factors

Content:

Explanation:
First, we decompose all of the terms into their prime factors. The [MATH: 20] in the numerator becomes [MATH: 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 5,] and the [MATH: 8(z-1)] in the denominator becomes [MATH: 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot (z-1).]

[MATH: (20)/(8(z − 1)) = (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 5)/(2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (z − 1))]

Then, we cancel out all the pairs of common factors in the numerator and denominator. In this case, there are two pairs of [MATH: 2]'s.

[MATH: (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 5)/(2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (z − 1))|=; (2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 5)/(2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ (z − 1))|=; (5)/(2 ⋅ (z − 1))|=; (5)/(2(z − 1))]
